We have [MATH: n=40, \widehat{\,p} = 0.3,] and we wish to construct a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p.]

Content:
To construct our confidence interval, the first thing to do is to establish the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

Content:
Since the United States has around [MATH: 240] million registered voters, the sample size [MATH: n=40] is clearly less than [MATH: 10\%] of the population size. This means that, provided certain conditions are met, the following approximation can be applied:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right)]

Content:
Let's check that our usual conditions hold in this case (where we use [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] as an estimate for [MATH: p]):

Content:
[MATH: np^(^)|= 40 ⋅ 0.3; = 12; > 5✓; n(1 − p^(^))|= 40 ⋅ (1 − 0.3); = 28; > 5✓]

Content:
Since all three conditions hold, the above approximation is applicable.

Content:
By transforming [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] to a standard normal random variable, we have

Content:
[MATH: Z= \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})/n}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
We wish to find a [MATH: z]-interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: Z] lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ef967288e591c11ee1cd7f20f6d79eaf]

Content:
To help with the notation, we define a new parameter [MATH: \alpha.] Since we're computing a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval, we have

Content:
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as [MATH: \pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/80c46885c5c97f5627cbd2e2adb6577b]

Content:
According to our diagram,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.]

Content:
Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that [MATH: z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(− 1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95.]

Content:
Therefore, there is a [MATH: 95\%] probability that our random variable [MATH: Z] will lie in the interval [MATH: (-1.96, 1.96).]

Content:
Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population proportion [MATH: p\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 1.96|< Z < 1.96; − 1.96|< (p^(^) − p)/(sqrt(p^(^)(1 − p^(^))/n)) < 1.96; − 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n))|< p^(^) − p < 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n)); − p^(^) − 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n))|< − p < − p^(^) + 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n)); p^(^) + 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n))|> p > p^(^) − 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n)); p^(^) − 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n))|< p < p^(^) + 1.96 ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n))]

Content:
Therefore, a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: {p}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(
\widehat{\,p} -1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}},\:
\widehat{\,p} +1.96 \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}

\right).]

Content:
Finally, substituting our values

Content:
[MATH: n=40, \qquad
\widehat{\,p}=0.3,]

Content:
we obtain that our [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for [MATH: {p}] is

Content:
[MATH: \big( 0.3 - 0.142, \: 0.3 + 0.142 \big)]

Content:
which simplifies to

Content:
[MATH: \big( 0.158, \: 0.442 \big).]

Content:
Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure.

Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=100] from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.64,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.

[IMG: /graphics/0ce9e4b15b73a3280cbe84f5627eadf1]

Consider a sample of size [MATH: n=100] from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.64,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: n=100] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}=0.64,] we have that

  • [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} = 100 \cdot 0.64 = 64 > 5,] and

  • [MATH: n(1-\widehat{\,p}) = 100 \cdot (1-0.64) = 36 > 5.]

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})/n}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,

  • [MATH: p] is the population proportion, and

  • [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of the original distribution can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] is the following:

[MATH: 0.64 ± 1.645 ⋅ sqrt((0.64(1 − 0.64))/(100)); 0.64 ± 0.079]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's now discuss how to construct a confidence interval for the proportion of the population whose members have a particular characteristic.

Content:
As a concrete example, let [MATH: p] represent the proportion of the United States voting population that will vote for candidate [MATH: A] in the next presidential election.

Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n=40] from our population. After processing our results, we find that the proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] of sample members that plan to vote for candidate [MATH: A] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} = 0.3.]

Content:
This is our estimate of the population proportion [MATH: p.]

Content:
Of course, the quantity that we're really interested in is [MATH: p,] the proportion of the entire voting population that will vote for candidate [MATH: A.] We want to get an idea of how accurate our estimate is. Therefore, we wish to construct a confidence interval of the form

Content:
[MATH: (\widehat{\,p}-E, \: \widehat{\,p}+E),]

Content:
where [MATH: E] is some margin of error.

Content:
Let's now discuss how to construct a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Constructing Confidence Intervals

Content:
We have [MATH: n=40, \widehat{\,p} = 0.3,] and we wish to construct a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p.]

Content:
To construct our confidence interval, the first thing to do is to establish the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.]

Content:
Since the United States has around [MATH: 240] million registered voters, the sample size [MATH: n=40] is clearly less than [MATH: 10\%] of the population size. This means that, provided certain conditions are met, the following approximation can be applied:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \sim N\left( p, \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \right)]

Content:
Let's check that our usual conditions hold in this case (where we use [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] as an estimate for [MATH: p]):

Content:
[MATH: np^(^)|= 40 ⋅ 0.3; = 12; > 5✓; n(1 − p^(^))|= 40 ⋅ (1 − 0.3); = 28; > 5✓]

Content:
Since all three conditions hold, the above approximation is applicable.

Content:
By transforming [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] to a standard normal random variable, we have

Content:
[MATH: Z= \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})/n}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
We wish to find a [MATH: z]-interval that we're [MATH: 95\%] confident that the random variable [MATH: Z] lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ef967288e591c11ee1cd7f20f6d79eaf]

Content:
To help with the notation, we define a new parameter [MATH: \alpha.] Since we're computing a [MATH: 95\%] confidence interval, we have

Content:
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as [MATH: \pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/80c46885c5c97f5627cbd2e2adb6577b]

Content:
According to our diagram,

Content:

Item 3 — Tutorial: Confidence Intervals for Proportions

Content:
Suppose we have a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a sufficiently large population with sample proportion [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.] Let's also assume that the following conditions are satisfied:

Content:
- [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} > 5]
- [MATH: n (1-\widehat{\,p}) > 5]

Content:
Then, for a given value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] a [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \left(
\widehat{\,p} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}},\:

\widehat{\,p} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}
\right).]

Content:
The endpoints of our confidence interval are the confidence limits and are given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}.]

Content:
Each part of the formula above has a name:

Content:
- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion
- [MATH: n] is the sample size
- [MATH: z_{\alpha/2}] is the corresponding [MATH: z]-score
- [MATH: E = z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}] is the margin of error

Content:
[MATH: z]

Content:
So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (p^(^) − [margin of error],|p^(^) + [margin of error]); (p^(^) − [[math]z[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error],|p^(^) + [[math]z[/math]-score] ⋅ [standard error]); (p^(^) − z_{α/2} ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n)),|p^(^) + z_{α/2} ⋅ sqrt((p^(^)(1 − p^(^)))/(n)))]

Content:
Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.

Content:
Finally, in the future, you may assume that if a population is "large," it is sufficiently larger than any sample drawn from it.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:

- [MATH: n \widehat{\,p} = 100 \cdot 0.64 = 64 > 5,] and
- [MATH: n(1-\widehat{\,p}) = 100 \cdot (1-0.64) = 36 > 5.]

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

[MATH: \dfrac{\widehat{\,p} - p}{\sqrt{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})/n}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}] is the sample proportion,
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion, and
- [MATH: n] is the sample size.

Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] of the original distribution can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the population proportion [MATH: p] is the following:

[MATH: 0.64 ± 1.645 ⋅ sqrt((0.64(1 − 0.64))/(100)); 0.64 ± 0.079]
